claims.text: Toughness retention in tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloys is governed by a balance between beneficial nanocrystalline grain boundaries and deleterious Cr/V-rich precipitates.
A high density of grain boundaries promotes uniform defect recombination.
Cr and V segregate at grain boundaries and form nanoscale precipitates.
Crossing a critical thermal threshold causes precipitate formation that locally embrittles the matrix and degrades toughness.
Magnetron sputtering can produce a quaternary W-Ta-V-Cr alloy with a single-phase BCC structure.
Approximately 70% of the grains in the deposited W-Ta-V-Cr alloy are 100 nm or smaller.
The initial W-Ta-V-Cr material has minimal precipitate formation.
Annealing at 1073 K, relative to 973 K, induces enhanced Cr/V segregation and precipitation.
Thermal annealing of the W-Ta-V-Cr alloy has been performed at temperatures up to 1073 K.
The relevant Cr- and V-rich grain-boundary precipitates are 3–5 nm in size.
At annealing temperatures at or below 1023 K, grain boundaries support balanced diffusion and uniform defect recombination.
Balanced diffusion and uniform defect recombination at or below 1023 K maintain toughness.
At 1073 K, kinetic effects promote Cr/V segregation and precipitation at grain boundaries.
Cr/V-rich grain-boundary precipitates cause local embrittlement despite retention of a fine-grained structure.
Samples annealed at 1073 K will have a higher grain-boundary precipitate density than samples annealed at 973 K.
Samples annealed at 1073 K will have lower fracture toughness and ductility than samples annealed at 973 K.
As-deposited samples or samples annealed at temperatures at or below 1023 K retain toughness through efficient defect recombination.
The proposed mechanism should apply to similarly nanostructured, high-grain-boundary-density, BCC tungsten-based refractory HEAs.
The proposed mechanism may not apply to coarse-grained alloys or alloys with markedly different chemistry.
